body: Another problem is that in post-Saussurian concepts of difference, and in the traditions of phenomenology and psychoanalysis with which the linguistic turn interacts, there is an insufficient understanding of multiplicity and emergence. Difference tends to be confined to relationality, and relationality to the relationship between two separate things. In Derrida difference is what disturbs binaries from within. For Deleuze, instead, difference consists of an open field of differentiations which only seldom express themselves as binaries. Hence, in postcolonial theory following Fanon and Said, as well as in structuralism,
there is a tendency to conceive
and more such splits and bifurcations, even while the liberal mainstream for understanding these binaries as metaphysical is rigorously critiqued
is always already related to what it is not, or to what will negate it in a next step of unfolding

. For the dialectic, difference is per definition grasped only insofar as it pertains to the self-developing realm of human subjectivity and language, or to what is since the mid-1990s called discourse.

Now, there is nothing simplistic about this concept of difference. The sophisticated poststructuralist conceptualizations of twoness in postcolonial theory are a culmination of a long and venerable legacy going back to Hegel. But for Deleuze this difference restrains thinking difference ‘in itself’, as an emergent process of many things interacting, unshackled by some prior negation, and greatly exceeding what can be grasped of it by discourse and ideas. To repeat, I am giving the argument in a nutshell here, and there is no place here to go into the hugely interesting tension between Hegel and Deleuze, a debate which has immediate ramifications for how racial and colonial differences are conceived.Footnote14 For now let us remember Deleuze's Difference and Repetition engages unabashedly in ontology, into what reality is. For post-Derridean theorists today, instead, and especially perhaps postcolonial theory, this move to ontology is already deemed illegitimately ambitious, and hence Eurocentric.

It is therefore no surprise it is only a few who use Deleuze to retheorize empire or literatures from the Global South.Footnote15 In his elegant critique of our collection Peter Kulchyski goes through the motion of reminding us Deleuze was a white male. This is redundant.
Postcolonial theory, civil rights theory and gender theory
As Fanon understood so well, and as can be seen in the Haitian Revolution,
at the very time it was becoming more entwined with other continents
. Together with the evil of colonialism, these good things spread to and changed the rest of the world.
It is not just that these European legacies
are worth fighting for—that is, they
require that any revolutionary politics worth its salt must
That one has to apologize for engaging in abstraction, ontology and science has
effect of cultural relativism, multiculturalism and the tiresome epistemology of positionality.

Deleuze and Race can be criticized for having focused so much on the theoretical effort of removing representationalism from the conceptualization of race that too little was formulated for activating and mobilizing antiracism. Swanton especially desires a more forceful and practical politics. This is a valid criticism, but
the question is how we define politics

. In one way politics is everywhere in the book, since the materialist approach to race immediately exposes the potentialities for transformation. But maybe this exposing should be called theoretico-ethics, not politics as such. Maybe it is true the book contains too much description and not enough prescription. It does not provide a toolbox for organizing protest movements, occupations and pressure groups against the racial order (for example, Black Lives Matter, the international solidarity movement for Palestine, networks for climate justice, groups of landless peasants or indigenous tribes in India or Brazil). It would be wrong, however, to suppose the book is therefore irrelevant to politics.
a theoretical taking stock of the field in which it is to intervene
work remains content to celebrate differences and multiplicities

. We should take seriously Guattari's passionate calls for the militant subversion of the way things are. Deleuze and Guattari are often caricaturized as the quintessential joyful affirmers of the cosmos as it is, like some kind of anarcho-Epicurean mystics. Any careful reader knows that what their work affirms and is joyful about is in fact the difficult commitment to the active deterritorialization, even destruction, of the sad and reactive machines keeping humans in their places. Such a revolutionary version of Spinozism, which Deleuze and Guattari share with Negri, poses the question of how collectivities can reinvent life.

My reading of Deleuze is therefore definitely further to the left than the influential Deleuzians Swanton cites (Grosz, Massumi, Protevi, Connolly), insofar as these do not sufficiently take up Deleuze and Guattari's critiques of global capitalism. What is needed is a movement I have no hesitation calling communism, following Guattari and Negri.Footnote17 After all, since the driver responsible for faciality and the racial order in the first place is capital, there can be no overcoming of racism without dismantling the current mode of production. In contrast, most Deleuzians do not explicitly distinguish between ethics, politics and aesthetics. I position them politically as something like social-democratic pluralists. Meanwhile the more extravagant celebrations of desire and difference come closer to anarchism, so are too left for me. It is true Deleuze and Guattari should have been clearer about their politics. Even if their theory of reterritorialization is meant to emphasize how easily capitalism and biopower absorb subversion and critique, they are relatively vague on how revolutionary movements are to avoid this.
micropolitics tends to tip into ethics and dissolve the political as such

Like in 1980s cultural studies, some Anglophone theoretical circles today have the tendency to call a critical analysis of a movie scene or an interactive performance piece ‘political’ by virtue of its alleged subversive qualities. However clever,
is not enough to upend the crises of financial collapse
A start in clearly defining politics as such requires conceiving it as a force, locally gathering bodies in order to globally jam the ideologies which prevent system change
. I follow Badiou in conceiving politics, science, art and love as autonomous trajectories which, as such, provide the basis for philosophy.Footnote18
Racist patriarchy will not disappear because of art, however much it can inspire militants to fight the power
Politics has its own affects and movements
, and this is something Deleuze and Guattari did not pay sufficient attention to.

Another criticism Swanton levels at the book is its disorganized, or at the least rhizomatic content. Jason Michael Adams and I tried to achieve resonances and variations across chapters, which I think we achieved more than most of the collections in the ‘Deleuze Connections’ book series, but perhaps not enough. Still, edited collections are as a rule without much overlap between chapters. The singularity of topic and approach is precisely what most collections are about (especially if some authors are known figures … ). When Swanton wishes for a more linear or structured introduction to the question of Deleuze and race he is wishing for a monograph, and forgets that editors are not meant to be picking (or rewriting) chapters so as to better align them. In fact, I should take the opportunity here to repeat my earlier point, that extremely little work on Deleuze and race exists. This is mostly because, as Swanton notes and I have been explaining, critical race theory and postcolonial studies are heavily anchored in more representationalist philosophies. What you see of authors in this book comes therefore after a considerable amount of searching.

Finally, Swanton questions the efficacy of the book in convincing scholars of race (and we can add, of colonialism) that Deleuzian ontology is crucial for overcoming the political and conceptual pitfalls in their work. Peter Kulchyski too laments the fact the book barely engages venerable theorists of race like Stuart Hall, bell hooks and W.E.B. Dubois. Yet both criticisms at the same time intuit that the book seeks to convince Deleuze scholars to think about race, not race scholars to read Deleuze, though I would certainly hope the latter happens, since they are far more numerous! More particularly, Swanton says it is a ‘real shame’ that the ‘obtuse’ and ‘faddish’ nature of the book prevents a steady dissemination of Deleuzian concepts within the study of race and racism. There is behind this criticism a sentiment so old—the mainstream cannot understand your jargon hence it has no right to truth—that it barely warrants me addressing it, were it not for that it allows me to remind readers of two things.

First, it is true Deleuze and more so Guattari are probably the most extravagant of experimenters with style and concept creation ever to be called philosophers in their lifetime. It is also true the secondary literature sometimes emulates them too slavishly, an uncreative kind of fidelity which they themselves do not endorse. But Deleuze and Race shows precisely that obtuse terms can help retheorize and repoliticize important real-world problems. So second, with rampant anti-intellectualism defining the public sphere across the world (and it must be remembered here how Deleuze himself denounced the stupidity of electronic communication), it is our responsibility as intellectuals to resist the shame that the mainstream tries to impose on difficult writing, provided, of course, that the jargon be the means whereby society is critiqued and new concepts are created, not an end in itself. This is not to say Swanton is anti-intellectualist (much less stupid). Rather, we must take care not to make transparency and lack of jargon prerequisites for innovative work.

Perhaps the book should not have been in the ‘Deleuze Connections’ series, then. But imagine such a series, growing at an intemperate rate—Deleuze and … and … and … and … (I urge readers to browse all titles)—without a book on race. At the end of the day, books have their nooks, their milieus and niches. This one happens to be written for Deleuze studies. It has no responsibility to lay out the differences with other theorists of race (Gilroy, Goldberg, Winant, etc.), or even to introduce readers to Deleuzian terminology. Readers know they have to pair this book with others.

Let us return once more to politics. When Anna Secor writes that ‘antiracist politics can thus be built not on the argument for sameness but on the multiplicity of difference itself’, I am reminded of a small-but-big shift I made since calling for ‘a thousand tiny races’ and a subversive ‘molecular revolution’ within the whiteness of psychedelic counterculture.Footnote19 There indeed should be an antiracist proliferation of miscegenations and cross-pollinations, consistently following the ontology of Difference and Repetition, but only in the spheres of art and interpersonal love and friendship: Rimbaud, Césaire, Basquiat, Kahlo, Grace Jones, Prince. As I spell out in the introduction to Deleuze and Race, I now think the Deleuzian dismantling of race has to be supplemented with the clarity, even voluntarism, associated with the communist tradition.

This clarity is most systematically formulated by Deleuze's most formidable ontological rival today, Alain Badiou. In his Ethics Badiou provocatively calls for a politics of the Same, that is, of the universal capacity of humans to be touched by a rupture out of the banality of difference, against an ethics of proliferation which has become fundamental to liberal-capitalist democracies and academic circles.Footnote20
Antiracism has to have an ever-renewed universalizing aspect
. It is crucial to understand that
is something to be made and

of Christianity, humanism and (neo)liberalism. Badiou understands why poststructuralist theorists, including those in postcolonial or decolonial and feminist vein, had to critique the Enlightenment's political naivetés and ideological closures.
Universalizability is not given as some transhistorical, quasi-divine guarantee
It is revolutionary in that it discovers and extends potentialities for justice which are ideologically kept from view

the philosophers associated with these notions (Plato, Kant, Hegel—but not Marx and Freud). Still, it is possible to construct a Deleuzian defence of revolutionary universalism by way of many concepts in his arsenal, like geophilosophy, becoming, the people-to-come, a life, object = x and absolute deterritorialization. Just like in the communist tradition, Deleuze and Guattari are entirely clear throughout their oeuvres that capitalism's immanent universalization cannot help creating the conditions for a different and better system. This ‘belief in the world'—a notion well-known to Deleuzians—is a militant fidelity to always return to the possibility of the absolutely new, and what can stage a rapprochement of sorts with Badiou.Footnote21
politics capable of subverting structural and environmental racism globally
. It gave up on Frantz Fanon's belief in the world.

it is the scream for a new
. This includes the neocolonial incursions China is perpetrating into the African continent, a clear challenge to the binaries of postcolonial theorizing.
The responsibility of theorists is to create new conceptual platforms for a universalizing politics worthy of the planetary tsunamis of capitalist disaster
. The essays in Deleuze and Race and the critiques Michele Lobo was so kind to garner in this issue are parts of this urgent larger process.
